newsitem.title: USA: Clinton rides feel-good economy in re-election bid.
newsitem.headline: Clinton rides feel-good economy in re-election bid.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

Four years after heeding the celebrated campaign slogan of political guru James Carville and winning the U.S. presidency, Bill Clinton is again betting that "it's the economy, stupid" that decides elections.

With a hefty lead in the opinion polls in the waning days of the campaign, Democrat Clinton looks like an odds-on favourite to win re-election on November 5, and analysts credit the upbeat economy as a major factor.
"People are feeling good and they don't see any reason to change," said David Wyss, chief financial economist at Massachusetts-based consultants DRI/McGraw Hill.

That is the mirror image of the situation four years ago, when Clinton wrested the presidency from George Bush by "focusing like a laser" -- as he himself liked to put it -- on an economy widely perceived by voters to be struggling.
Economic growth did slow sharply in the third quarter of this year, a fact that Clinton's Republican rival Bob Dole jumped on on Wednesday in his last-ditch bid to revive his lagging campaign.

"It is disastrous news for American workers and businesses," Dole told supporters in Tennessee after a government report that growth fell to a 2.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter from 4.7 percent in the second.
But analysts said that it is inflation and jobs, rather than economic growth per se, that shapes voters' attitudes.
And on that score Clinton has much to crow about.

The so-called misery index -- which combines inflation and unemployment and has been used by candidates to belabor their rivals since Jimmy Carter popularised it 20 years ago -- is at its lowest level for a presidential election since 1968.
"It is near Nirvana for President Clinton," said David Orr, economist for the First Union Corp, a banking group based in Charlotte, North Carolina.
Perhaps mindful of that, Dole and his advisers have sought to shift the focus of the economic debate in the campaign to the long-run health of the economy.

They argue that the cyclical recovery that the United States is currently enjoying is sub-par and that the underlying economy has deteriorated, not improved, under Clinton. Their prescription to cure those ills: hefty tax cuts, government deregulation and a balanced federal budget.
"If this is a recovery, I can hardly wait for the recession," Dole said on Wednesday.
To buttress their view, Dole and his fellow Republicans have compared the economy's performance under Clinton to that under some past presidents -- and found it wanting.

Growth has averaged about 2-1/2 percent per year during Clinton's tenure. That is well short of the 4.5 percent annual pace from 1982 to 1987, when Ronald Reagan was president, or the 6.2 percent rate from 1961 to 1966, when John Kennedy and Lyndon Johnson were in the White House.
John Taylor, Dole's chief economic adviser, has tried to drive the point home by trotting out what he has dubbed the "economic progress" index as a rival to the misery index.

The new index measures the growth of productivity -- the value of goods or services produced per hour of work. That is important because it determines the long-run growth of the economy, and ultimately workers' wages.
Since Clinton took office in 1993, productivity has grown at a meagre 0.3 percent annual rate -- well below the one percent plus pace under presidents Reagan and Bush.
"That is close to the zero growth of pre-Industrial Revolution days," Taylor said, adding, "At that rate it would take 10 generations to double a person's income."

Even some of Clinton's supporters admit the economy has a long-term growth problem. But they argue that the president's plan for a balanced budget with targeted investment in education, training and technology is the answer to those long-term woes, not Dole's tax cut proposal.
